analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax on inherited wealth, recouping part of the revenue through capital gains taxes when heirs sell.
analysis.headline: The bill had 31 Senate backers, including 10 Democrats, but the Finance Committee never acted on it and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for anyone dying after enactment [S3]. The estate tax applies only above an exemption that was $650,000 in 1999 and scheduled to reach $1 million by 2006, so only estates above those levels were ever taxed [S3]. To make up part of the lost revenue, the bill would end the 'step-up in basis' rule, meaning heirs would inherit the deceased's original purchase price for tax purposes and owe capital gains tax when they sell inherited property [S2] [S3]. Executors would have to document that original basis for the Treasury and every beneficiary, with penalties for failures or false statements [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates above the exemption levels, who currently owe estate tax of up to 55% on the excess; the repeal would let them inherit the full value tax-free. Family-owned businesses and farms get an additional basis exclusion of up to $1.3 million. Wealth-advisory services built around estate tax planning lose their central reason to exist, since the tax would be gone.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely for estates of people dying after enactment, so heirs owe nothing on the inheritance itself [S3].

Ends the step-up in basis and instead lets heirs step basis up to fair market value only out of a limited 'exclusion allowance' — $650,000 in 1999, rising to $1 million by 2006, plus up to $1.3 million more for family-owned business interests — so gains beyond that are taxed as capital gains only when the heir sells, not as an estate tax on the whole estate upfront [S3].
Excludes up to $50,000 of tangible personal property and surviving-spouse transfers from the new capital gains regime, easing the transition for smaller bequests [S3].

analysis.who_pays: General federal taxpayers, who would fund the lost estate tax revenue through deficits or other taxes. Heirs, including those from more modest estates, would face new recordkeeping: executors must report each asset's original basis to the Treasury and to every beneficiary, with fines up to $5,000 for failures and penalties of 10% or 30% of any overstated basis [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and heirs with new paperwork

drawbacks.text: The repeal eliminates the entire transfer tax system while replacing only part of the revenue through the carryover basis rules, so the difference comes out of federal finances [S2] [S3].

The carryover basis system shifts tax from a levy few estates ever paid into capital gains tax that heirs owe at sale, and it imposes new compliance duties on every executor — filing information returns and facing fixed penalties for negligent or fraudulent overstatement of basis [S3].

Because basis tracking is done at death and binding on the Treasury if not challenged within set windows, disputes over a decedent's old purchase records would fall on families and the executor, creating a new source of audits and Tax Court proceedings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For very large estates the benefit is straightforward and large: no estate tax at all. The offsetting carryover basis means heirs owe capital gains on old appreciation only when they sell, at lower rates than the estate tax, and families below the exemption amounts — the vast majority — gain little and take on new paperwork. The honest accounting: this is a major tax cut concentrated at the top, partially paid for by a compliance-heavy capital gains regime that reaches smaller inheritances, with the remaining revenue gap left to other taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never reported it or scheduled any action, so it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2001 without ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the bill on May 26, 1999 with six original cosponsors, including two Democrats (Sens. Kerrey and Breaux), and it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee the same day [S1] [S5] [S3].
Thirty senators cosponsored the bill — 10 Democrats and 20 Republicans — yet the Finance Committee never took it up [S4] [S5].
Kyl delivered introductory remarks again on September 5, 2000, over a year after referral, but no committee or floor action followed [S5].
The bill's final action in the record is that second set of remarks; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury and general taxpayers, who kept the estate tax on very large inheritances rather than absorbing the lost revenue. Heirs of large estates did not win repeal through this bill, though the same idea returned in later Congresses.

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on the floor in 1999 and again in 2000, and recruited cosponsors [S1] [S5].

for.name: Sen. Bob Kerrey
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the estate tax repeal bipartisan sponsorship [S3] [S4].

against.name: Sen. William Roth
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it, held no markup on it, and never scheduled it, so it never reached the Senate floor [S5].

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: In 2000 he vetoed the House-passed estate tax repeal (H.R. 8), the companion to this bill, and the Senate failed to override, removing the political path for repeal in the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 31 senators, including 10 of the 45 Democrats — but with the bill stuck in committee, no roll-call ever tested where the chamber stood.

industries.note: The estate tax applies only above a $650,000-to-$1 million exemption, so repeal delivers its entire benefit to the estates above that line, while the revenue loss spreads across all taxpayers. Had the bill passed, the largest inheritances would owe nothing on the transfer itself [S3].

The bill adds a separate $1.3 million basis exclusion for family-owned business interests, on top of the general exclusion, giving owners of sizable farms and closely held firms an extra buffer from the replacement capital gains tax [S3].

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: The estate tax drives a large planning industry of trusts, valuations, and filings; outright repeal would eliminate the problem those services exist to manage. The new carryover-basis paperwork would replace some of that work with a different, simpler compliance task [S3].
